practice: Care for older and dying people

models.best: Inferred from its principle that gifts create duties to return, older and dying people are cared for by kin and neighbours who expect care back in later years, so care rests on trust and standing rather than fees. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that favours create duties to return, care follows kinship and alliance, so people without kin or standing in a network receive little care and have no fixed claim to it. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Sahlins, Stone Age Economics

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a household balances its work against its needs, so older people stay in the family home and receive care from the household's own labour, sized to what the family can spare. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that production serves consumption, so a household with few working members cannot spare labour for care, leaving one or two carers with the whole load and sometimes forcing a move away from home. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Chayanov, The Theory of Peasant Economy

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a central authority collects goods and redistributes them to workers and officials, so care for older and dying people can be paid from a common store and provided through central institutions. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the centre allocates goods by office and service, so older people outside the service of officials receive little, and care depends on rank and favour rather than on need. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Polanyi, The Great Transformation

models.best: Inferred from its principle that owners bear the cost of maintaining the people they own, so food and shelter are provided on the estate for as long as the owner can draw labour from them. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that enslaved people are denied property and education, so older people have no savings, no claim to land or family wealth, and no right to care once they can no longer work. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Williams, Capitalism and Slavery

models.best: Inferred from its principle that tenants owe services for land, protection and justice, so an older tenant keeps a holding and a place on the manor, supplied from the manor's own produce. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that land is held in return for labour services, so an older tenant who can no longer work may lose the holding and the protection tied to it, and must depend on family. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Bloch, Feudal Society

models.best: Inferred from its principle that guilds regulate training and quality under statute, so carers are trained to a set standard and older people receive care from members whose skill the trade checks. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that guilds regulate entry and prices, so new carers wait long to be admitted to the trade, prices are set by the masters, and older people and families have fewer providers to choose from. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Epstein, Freedom and Growth

models.best: Inferred from its principle that the state aims for a surplus and regulates production toward national gain, so public funds support family care where it keeps members in work and the national workforce healthy. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state regulates trade toward national gain, so care for older people is funded only from what remains once trade and state aims are met, and public homes and carers receive less than productive trades. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Heckscher, Mercantilism

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a single tax on the rent of land funds the state, so public care for older people can be paid from land values without taxing labour or the goods that families buy. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that only agriculture creates a net product, so care work, counted as producing none, goes unfunded and falls on families and on the charity of landowners. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Meek, The Economics of Physiocracy

models.best: Inferred from its principle that competition among private providers raises quality and lowers prices, so homes and home-care firms compete for older people's custom while the state only enforces the contracts they sign. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Leaving care homes to private owners, with the state only enforcing contracts, is this model's risk. The case Private equity ownership of nursing homes studied more than 12,400 for-profit skilled nursing facilities, 1,674 of them bought by private equity firms. The NBER digest describes an association: mortality during a stay and in the 90 days after it was about 10 per cent higher at private equity-owned facilities. No null or positive result for the other side appears in the results. Source: Gupta and colleagues, NBER Working Paper 28474, summarised in an NBER digest (2021); study of private equity-backed nursing homes in COVID-19, as cited in secondary write-ups

models.best: Inferred from its principle that prices carry knowledge spread across many people, so care prices and service types signal what older people and families want, and no planner has to judge how many places to provide. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that credit expansion distorts production, so cheap credit for building or buying care homes can start a boom in capacity that later falls, leaving homes closed and residents moved mid-care. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Hayek, The Use of Knowledge in Society

models.best: Inferred from its principle that privatised provision and a smaller state let families choose among competing homes and home-care firms, with public money going where the family chooses rather than to fixed budgets. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Privatisation of care homes to financial owners, with fewer controls, is this model's risk. The case Private equity ownership of nursing homes studied more than 12,400 for-profit skilled nursing facilities, 1,674 of them bought by private equity firms. The NBER digest describes an association: mortality during a stay and in the 90 days after it was about 10 per cent higher at private equity-owned facilities. No null or positive result for the other side appears in the results. Source: Gupta and colleagues, NBER Working Paper 28474, summarised in an NBER digest (2021); study of private equity-backed nursing homes in COVID-19, as cited in secondary write-ups

models.best: Public funding for care, which this model supports, is shown by the case Japan's long-term care insurance, from 2000: a 2017 article credits it with easing the strain on families who care for relatives, but it reports views and judgments, not measured outcomes.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that government spending falls in booms, so places and grants for home care are cut in strong years and widened only in slumps, leaving older people and carers exposed to the business cycle. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Keynes, The General Theory

models.best: Shared social insurance, which this model favours, is shown by the case Germany's long-term care insurance, from 1995: employers and workers shared its cost equally, home care was paid from April 1995 and residential care from July 1996. Evaluation sources are thin: one essay and one 2003 catalogue record.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that a legal order curbs monopoly, so if that order is weak, a few insurers or care firms could dominate local supply and set the terms of care for older people and families, who then have little choice. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Müller-Armack, Wirtschaftslenkung und Marktwirtschaft

models.best: Inferred from its principle that universal public services, financed by high taxes, give every older and dying person care as a right, with home help and nursing places run by public bodies. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that high taxes fund universal services, so care capacity depends on the tax base, and when public employers cannot recruit enough staff at national pay, waiting for home help and nursing places grows. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Esping-Andersen, The Three Worlds of Welfare Capitalism

models.best: Inferred from its principle that the state directs funds to chosen fields and disciplines firms by performance, so public money for care homes and home services is steered to providers that meet set targets and are paid for results. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state picks favoured fields, so care for older people, which is not a chosen export industry, gets less attention and funding, and the sector can be left short of capital. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Johnson, MITI and the Japanese Miracle

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a tax on the value of land funds public services, so care homes and home-care services can be paid for from land rents, and speculation that drives up the cost of sites for homes falls. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that land value is taxed rather than labour and capital, so funding for care depends on land values, and public care is thinnest in areas where land is cheap and rents are low. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: George, Progress and Poverty

models.best: Inferred from its principle that cooperative communities built by example replace wage competition, so older people live in shared communities where members look after each other and the dying are not left alone. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that communities are built by example and voluntary membership, so care depends on whether a community has enough members willing to give time, and older people in small or failed communities have no fallback. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Fourier, Le Nouveau Monde industriel

models.best: Inferred from its principle that mutual credit and free contracts let members keep the full value of their work, so mutual societies lend at cost and pay for care from shared funds that members have built. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that rent on property is abolished and banks lend at cost, so a mutual fund for care has no property base to draw on in a crisis, and members who fall ill or grow old may find shared funds too thin to cover long care. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Proudhon, What Is Property?

models.best: Inferred from its principle that members own and control firms and share the surplus between users and workers, so a care cooperative can be owned and run by its carers and families, with users and workers sharing the surplus. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that one member one vote governs the firm, so a cooperative of carers may put staff pay ahead of the older people it serves, or the reverse, and a failing cooperative may leave residents without a provider. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Mondragón cooperatives

models.best: Inferred from its principle that with no wages and no state, goods are shared according to need within federated communes, so care is given where it is needed, by neighbours and communes, with no price and no contract. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that free association replaces contracts, so care depends on who is willing to give it, and an older or dying person in a commune with few willing helpers has no contract or fixed claim to care. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Kropotkin, The Conquest of Bread

models.best: Inferred from its principle that trade unions run industry through workers' organisations, so care work is organised by the carers' own unions, which bargain over staffing and training and can use strikes to defend both. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that unions use strikes and, eventually, a general strike, so care for older people can be disrupted when carers stop work, and the frail or dying lose services during a dispute. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Pelloutier, Histoire des Bourses du travail

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a national minimum of welfare is provided by municipal and national public enterprise, so every older person is guaranteed a basic level of home or residential care, run by public authorities. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that change comes gradually through public enterprise, so a minimum standard can be set while care above it waits for slow reform, and municipal homes may differ widely between towns. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Founding of the Fabian Society

models.best: Inferred from its principle that workers and consumers share control of industry through guild-like councils, so carers and families of older people sit on the councils that run homes and home-care services. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state is one partner among several, so care decisions may be split between councils, and an older person may find no body clearly responsible for the quality or funding of care. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Cole, Self-Government in Industry

models.best: Inferred from its principle that central plans set output and investment, so the state can build and staff homes and home-care services to a national target, and can mobilise labour for care where the need is greatest. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state sets output, prices and investment from the centre, so care follows plan targets rather than what older people need, and shortages of places and staff can persist until the plan is changed. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Kornai, The Socialist System

models.best: Inferred from its principle that public ownership with market prices has managers follow prices, while a central board sets the rules and the investment, so care homes are publicly owned and run to prices, with the board deciding how much capacity to build. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that a central board sets the rules and the investment, so if the board misjudges demand, care homes may run short of places or build more than older people need, and managers following prices may cut services that do not pay. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Yugoslav workers' self-management

models.best: Inferred from its principle that once classes disappear, distribution follows need, so older and dying people receive care according to need, paid from the common product rather than from wages or family means. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that distribution by need comes only after the state withers away, so during the transition care is allocated by the state and limited by what the economy can afford, and older people may wait while the principle is not yet met. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Marx, Critique of the Gotha Programme

models.best: Inferred from its principle that markets operate beside public ownership and reform proceeds in stages, so new forms of home care and residential care can be piloted in chosen cities before national rollout. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that reform is gradual and set under party direction, so older people in regions outside the chosen zones may wait longer for new services, and regional differences in care can widen as reform proceeds unevenly. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Naughton, The Chinese Economy

models.best: Inferred from its principle that workers' and consumers' councils plan through repeated proposals, so older people, carers and families propose and approve home and residential care, and care jobs are balanced in complexity across the workforce. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that neither markets nor central planners allocate, so care planning depends on repeated council rounds, which may be slow to respond to a sudden rise in need, and the dying may wait while proposals are revised. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Albert and Hahnel, Looking Forward

models.best: Inferred from its principle that employers and unions are organised into state-controlled corporations, so care providers and carers are placed in one coordinated plan for care capacity and training across the sector. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state directs industry toward national goals, including war, so care capacity and carers may be redirected to other priorities, and care for older people is cut when the state's goals require it. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Italian corporative law

models.best: Inferred from its principle that zakat redistributes wealth and trust underpins contracts, so zakat funds support older and dying people who have no means, and care arranged by contract rests on mutual trust. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that finance shares profit and risk, so providers of care funded through shared finance may be paid only when a home makes a surplus, and older people in low-yield areas may receive less care. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Chapra, Towards a Just Monetary System

models.best: Inferred from its principle that economic life serves well-being, so care for older and dying people is small-scale, local and unhurried, with moderate use of resources and attention given to the person rather than to speed. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that production is small-scale and local, so care in a sparsely populated area may be thin where few carers live, and moderation may limit investment in staff, equipment and places when demand grows. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Schumacher, Small Is Beautiful

models.best: Inferred from its principle that widespread private property and small enterprise give families a stake, so older people are cared for in small homes run by local owners, and subsidiarity keeps decisions with the smallest competent body. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that subsidiarity keeps decisions with the smallest competent body, so a small local body with few staff or funds may be unable to meet a rise in need, and no larger body is required to step in. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Belloc, The Servile State

models.best: Inferred from its principle that every person has a social floor within planetary limits, so every older and dying person has a basic right to care, and growth is not needed to pay for it. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that economic activity stays within planetary limits, so the care sector cannot grow without limit to meet a rise in the number of older people, and capacity may fall short of need when the population ages faster than the floor can be funded. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Raworth, Doughnut Economics

models.best: Inferred from its principle that every citizen receives an unconditional income, so older people and carers can buy care, or time off caring, without means tests, and families can choose where care is given. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the income is unconditional, so it does not by itself pay for care, and a basic income too low for care costs leaves older people to pay the rest from their own means, while taxes on land and natural resources must fund the scheme. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Van Parijs, Real Freedom for All

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a government which issues its own currency can fund full employment, so the state can pay for care homes and carers without a fixed borrowing limit, provided inflation is kept in check. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that inflation, not debt, is the real limit, so if public spending on care outruns the supply of care workers, prices for care and goods can rise, and older people on fixed incomes lose out. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Kelton, The Deficit Myth

models.best: Inferred from its principle that communities who share a resource govern it with rules they design, monitor and enforce, so a neighbourhood can manage shared care homes, gardens and carers' rotas under rules set by those who use them. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that a commons is nested in wider institutions, so a small community that runs care for older people without links to larger bodies may lack the staff, money or rules to cope with a rise in need or a serious case. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Ostrom, Governing the Commons

compromise.summary: A mixed scheme for care at home and in homes: employers and workers share a contribution, general taxes cover the rest, and public standards govern competing providers, with limits on how many homes one owner may hold and published staffing and death rates.
compromise.details: Keeps: shared employer and worker contributions, as in Germany's long-term care insurance, from 1995 (Social market economy); public funding that eases family strain, as in Japan's long-term care insurance, from 2000 (Keynesian welfare capitalism); competition among providers inside public rules, credited to Japan's scheme as a view, not a measured result (Social market economy). Blocks: private owners with few checks, which Private equity ownership of nursing homes links to higher mortality (Monetarist neoliberalism, Classical laissez-faire capitalism); safeguard: public approval of ownership changes and published mortality. One owner dominating a region (Social market economy); safeguard: a cap on homes per owner. Staff shortage and rising public costs, flagged in Japan's scheme; safeguard: a published staffing ratio and yearly cost review. Test: over five years from launch, compare 90-day mortality after admission, preventable emergency visits and carers' strain between approved and other homes. Source: vdek, history of long-term care insurance; Makiko Takao, 2017 article; Gupta and colleagues, NBER Working Paper 28474; Müller-Armack, Wirtschaftslenkung und Marktwirtschaft.
